title: Air Fryer Korean Sweet Potato (Goguma)
blurb: Caramelized, honey-sweet, fluffy inside. Walmart sells these as "Japanese" or "Korean" sweet potatoes — purple skin, pale flesh.
steps: Scrub potatoes. Pat dry. Rub all over with oil. Sprinkle with salt if using.
Skin should look wrinkled and caramelized. Fork slides in with no resistance.
Split open. Eat as-is, or top with butter and flaky salt.
notes: Goguma is sweeter and denser than orange sweet potatoes. The wrinkled skin is the doneness cue — pull too early and the center stays starchy.

title: Air Fryer Bulgogi
blurb: Pre-marinated Korean BBQ beef, fast in the air fryer. Caramelized edges, juicy inside. H Mart sells trays ready to cook.
appleNote: Check the marinade label for apple. H Mart's bulgogi marinade routinely uses pear and apple as tenderizers.

items: 6 leaves romaine or red leaf lettuce (optional, for ssam)

steps: Pat strips lightly with paper towel. Wet meat steams instead of searing. Leave some marinade clinging; that's flavor.
Parchment paper. Marinade drips burn onto the basket otherwise.
Spread meat in a single layer, not crowded. 1 lb usually needs 2 batches. 400°F for 6–8 min, shake or flip halfway.
Edges crisp and dark caramelized. Internal temp 145°F+.
2 min before plating. Serve over rice with kimchi, or ssam-style in lettuce wraps.
notes: Timings are for ~½" chunks (chuck eye roll). Thinner shavings: 4–5 min total. Thicker pieces: 8–10 min.
Sugar in the marinade burns above 400°F, so don't push the temp higher.
Leftovers reheat at 350°F, 2–3 min.

title: Sweet Red Bean Ongsimi (Microwave)
blurb: Microwave version of frozen Korean sweet rice dumpling porridge. Cozy, fast.
steps: Heat 280 mL water separately until boiling. Pour into a deep microwave-safe bowl.
Add ongsimis. Microwave on HIGH 3 min, stirring occasionally so they don't stick. They're ready when they float and feel firm.
Pour in the red bean porridge packet. Microwave on MEDIUM (50–60%) 5 more min, stirring well throughout — medium power prevents splattering.
notes: Use a deep bowl — this bubbles up aggressively. Adjust time based on microwave power. The porridge thickens as it cools.
Stovetop version: boil 280 mL water, cook ongsimi 3 min, add porridge packet, cook 5 min more.

title: Pork & Chive Mandoo
blurb: Korean pork and chive dumplings — a large batch of juicy filling, with an optional homemade wrapper.
locked: Sugar locked at 1 tbsp (10 Aug 2026). The source called for sugar in the steps but listed no amount; 1 tbsp against 1.5 kg pork is the standard balancing ratio.

items: 350 mL warm water — add up to 375 mL if needed

steps: Mix together hot water, ginger, salt, sugar, and MSG/Dashida.
Gradually add to pork until sticky.
Add in chives and mix until evenly combined.
Place 1 tbsp of filling onto wrapper and fold.
Divide dough into small pieces (~20–25 g each).
Roll each piece into a 3-inch circle.
notes: Sugar here is for balance, not sweetness; it rounds out the salt and MSG.
Pan-fry potsticker-style for the best texture — sear, add water, cover, steam, then re-crisp. See #12.
Freeze uncooked on a tray, then bag.

title: Kongguksu
blurb: Cold Korean noodle soup in a chilled, nutty soybean broth. A summer dish — served cold.
locked: Full ingredient list locked (10 Aug 2026). The original was lost; these are standard kongguksu ratios at 100 g dry noodles per person, not recovered originals.
steps: Blend soy milk, almonds, sesame seeds, and salt until completely smooth. Chill thoroughly — at least 2 hours.
Cook somyeon per package, usually 3–4 min. They cook fast; taste at 3.
Rinse under cold running water until the noodles are fully cold to the touch. Drain hard.
Divide noodles between two bowls. Pour the cold broth over.
Top with cucumber, egg halves, and sesame seeds.
notes: Soy milk must be unsweetened. Sweetened soy milk ruins this and there's no fixing it after.
Rinse the noodles until genuinely cold — residual heat turns the broth lukewarm and flat.
Salt to taste at the table is traditional; some people prefer it barely salted.

title: Potato Jeon
blurb: Crispy Korean potato pancakes made from blended fresh potato — chewy inside, golden outside.
locked: Starch and salt locked at 2 tbsp and ½ tsp (10 Aug 2026). Both were used in the source steps but absent from its ingredient list.
steps: Blend potato, onion, and water together. Strain through a wide sieve into a bowl.
Pour off the excess water from the strained liquid and add potato starch to the solids.
Medium heat, thin oil. Spoon in thin pancakes and cook 3–4 min per side until golden. Don't flip early.
notes: The starch that settles out of the strained liquid can replace or supplement packaged potato starch — let the drained liquid sit 10 minutes, pour off the water, and scrape the white paste from the bottom.
Thin pancakes crisp; thick ones go gummy in the middle.
#14 works as a dipping sauce here.

title: Shiroi Koibito Cookies
blurb: Langue de chat butter cookies sandwiching a white chocolate filling — the Hokkaido souvenir classic. Precision baking; the one genuinely fussy recipe in this book.
locked: Quantities locked at standard langue de chat ratios — roughly equal weights butter, sugar, and egg white (10 Aug 2026). Only the 5 g almond flour was confirmed from source. This is the one recipe where a wrong number actually breaks the result, so treat the first batch as a test.

items: 5 g flavoring powder (matcha or cocoa, optional)

steps: Electric whisk until the butter turns slightly pale.
Add room-temperature egg whites in several batches, mixing well between each.
Sift in cake flour and flavoring powder.
Fold in heavy cream until smooth.
Set up a square mold and pipe the mixture in.
Smooth the surface and lift the mold away.
Melt white chocolate over a double boiler at a bare simmer.
Pipe into square molds, smooth, freeze 20 minutes.
Sandwich the cookies, using melted white chocolate as glue.
notes: Use 4 g almond flour instead of 5 g when swapping in matcha or cocoa.
Egg whites must be at room temperature or the batter splits.
White chocolate scorches easily — keep the double boiler at a bare simmer, never a boil.
Walmart carries cake flour and almond flour in the baking aisle.

title: Sizzling Beef Pepper Rice
blurb: Pepper Lunch at home — thin beef, buttered rice, corn, and a lot of black pepper, all seared together in a hot pan.
locked: Quantities locked at standard ratios (10 Aug 2026). The source wrote "thin sliced meat" and "sweetener" without amounts; mirin chosen over sugar for the sweetener.

items: 1 tsp coarse black pepper, plus more to finish

steps: Combine soy sauce, mirin, and garlic. Set aside.
Cast iron or heavy skillet over high heat until genuinely hot. This dish depends on the sear.
Mound cooked rice in the center of the pan. Press the butter into the top.
Ring the rice with the beef and corn.
Leave undisturbed 1–2 min to brown the beef and crisp the rice bottom.
Pour sauce over. Toss everything together until the beef is just cooked through.
Heavy grind of black pepper and green onion. Serve immediately.
notes: The pan must be hotter than feels comfortable. Day-old cold rice crisps better than fresh.
Shabu-style beef from H Mart is the right cut; Walmart's thin sliced steak works in a pinch.

title: Chicken Katsu
blurb: Panko-crusted fried chicken, milk-marinated and breaded — written as a freezer meal-prep batch.
locked: Quantities locked at standard breading ratios for 4 cutlets (10 Aug 2026).

items: 4 chicken breasts, butterflied and pounded thin

steps: Submerge chicken in milk. Refrigerate at least 1 hour, ideally overnight. Milk tenderizes and mellows any gaminess.
Remove from milk, pat dry. Season both sides with salt and pepper.
Dredge in flour, then beaten egg, then press firmly into panko. Press hard — loose panko falls off in the oil.
Lay breaded cutlets flat on a parchment-lined tray. Freeze solid, then transfer to a bag. Cook from frozen.
350°F oil, 3–4 min per side from fresh. Golden brown, internal 165°F.
Rest 3 min on a rack, then slice crosswise into strips. Serve with tonkatsu sauce and rice.
notes: The out-of-order freezer step — breading before freezing, not after — is deliberate. It's what makes this a batch recipe.
For the air fryer version from frozen, see #11.
Rest on a rack, never a plate. A plate traps steam and softens the crust.

title: Rice Cooker Gyudon
blurb: Japanese beef bowl, dump-and-forget. Everything goes in at the start; no monitoring.

items: 1 cup water (reduced — the sauce adds liquid)
Pickled ginger (beni shoga), to serve — optional

steps: Rinse until the water runs mostly clear. Add to the rice cooker with the reduced water.
Stir together soy sauce, mirin, and sugar until the sugar dissolves.
Lay sliced onion over the rice, then the beef on top. Do not stir — layering keeps the rice from going gummy.
Pour sauce evenly over the top. Close the lid, run a standard white rice cycle.
When the cycle ends, leave on keep-warm 10 minutes before opening.
Meanwhile, fry an egg sunny-side up, or soft-boil one (6½ min from boiling).
Fluff gently, bowl it up, top with the egg and pickled ginger.
notes: Water is reduced to 1 cup because the sauce contributes liquid — don't use the rice cooker's normal fill line.
The egg is the one step that can't be hands-off. Drop it entirely for true zero-touch cooking; the dish still works.
Shabu-style beef from H Mart; Walmart's thin sliced steak, partially frozen and sliced thinner, is the fallback.

title: Air Fryer Frozen Pork Katsu
blurb: Prepped-and-frozen breaded pork cutlets straight from the freezer. No thawing.
steps: Spray both sides of each frozen cutlet. This is what browns the coating — skip it and the panko stays pale and floury.
Single layer, not touching. Cook in batches if needed.
Internal temp 145°F, or cut into the thickest point — no pink, juices clear.
Rest 3 min on a rack. Slice crosswise. Serve with tonkatsu sauce and shredded cabbage.
notes: Thickness is the whole variable. 18 min suits thin cutlets; thick ones need the full 22 or a few more. Once you've dialed in the number for your cutlets, record it here.
A paler coating than deep-fried katsu is normal for frozen breaded items — the panko has only circulating air to brown in. Judge by internal temp, not color.

title: Pan-Fried Pork & Chive Dumplings (Potsticker Style)
blurb: Crispy bottom, steamed top. The best method for frozen dumplings, full stop.
steps: Non-stick or cast iron over medium-high with a thin layer of oil.
Add frozen dumplings flat-side down. Sear 2–3 min until the bottoms are golden brown. Don't move them.
Pour in water and rice vinegar. Cover immediately. Steam 5–6 min until the water evaporates.
Uncover. Let the bottoms re-crisp 1–2 min. Slide onto a plate, crispy-side up.
notes: Rice vinegar in the steam water is the trick — it adds subtle tang and helps crisp the bottoms.
No need to thaw. Thawing makes them soggy and they'll tear.
Air fryer version: #13. Dipping sauce: #14.

title: Air Fryer Pork & Chive Dumplings
blurb: Convenience-focused. Crispy all over rather than just the bottom, but you lose the crisp/soft contrast.
steps: Toss frozen dumplings with oil so each is lightly coated. Non-negotiable — skipping it gives dry, tough skin.
Arrange in a single layer, not touching, pleats up. Cook 8–10 min, flipping at halfway. Spray or brush with water mid-cook to keep the wrappers from drying.
notes: Less mess than pan-frying, but you give up the crisp/soft contrast.
Spritz with water at the flip — wrappers dry out otherwise. A 1:1 water-and-oil brush instead of straight oil works even better.
Larger dumplings: add 2–3 min.
Stovetop version: #12. Dipping sauce: #14.

title: Simple Dumpling Dipping Sauce
blurb: Salty, tangy, nutty. Pairs with any dumpling method, and with potato jeon.
steps: Whisk everything together in a small bowl. Done.
notes: Skip the chili oil if you don't like heat. Add a pinch of sugar to round things out.
Julienned fresh ginger instead of grated is excellent if you don't mind the texture.
Goes with #4, #6, #12, and #13.

title: Rice Cooker Hainanese Chicken
blurb: Poached chicken and fragrant rice cooked in one appliance, with a sharp ginger-garlic sauce. Deceptively simple for how good it is.
locked: Quantities locked (10 Aug 2026). Garlic (10–12 cloves) and neutral oil (2–3 tbsp) were confirmed after two source cells came back as corrupted Excel date serials; the rest are standard ratios.
steps: Rinsed rice, broth, sliced ginger, and salt into the rice cooker pot. Stir once.
Lay chicken thighs skin-side up directly on top of the rice. Don't submerge — the fat renders down into the rice as it cooks.
Run a standard white rice cycle.
While that runs, combine minced garlic, grated ginger, and salt in a heatproof bowl. Heat the neutral oil until shimmering, then pour it over the aromatics — it will sizzle. Stir in sesame oil.
Leave on keep-warm 10 minutes after the cycle ends.
Chicken over the rice, cucumber alongside, sauce spooned over everything.
notes: Broth is deliberately reduced to a 1:1 ratio — the chicken releases a lot of liquid as it cooks.
Pouring genuinely hot oil over raw garlic is the whole point of the sauce. It cooks the raw edge off without frying it. Get the oil shimmering, not smoking.

title: One-Pot Chuck Beef Curry
blurb: Braised beef curry with potato and carrot. Gram-measured. Chuck is the right cut — it needs the long simmer.

items: 1 tsp cornstarch + 1 tbsp cold water (mixed together)

steps: Oil in a heavy pot over medium-high. Brown the beef on all sides, ~6 min. Work in batches if crowded. Remove and set aside.
Same pot, medium heat. Onion until translucent, ~5 min.
Add curry powder to the onion. Stir constantly 60 seconds until fragrant. This step is what separates good curry from dusty curry.
Return the beef. Add broth and soy sauce. Bring to a boil, then reduce to a low simmer, cover, 45 min.
Potato and carrot. Simmer uncovered 20–25 min until fork-tender.
Stir in the cornstarch slurry. Simmer 2 min until the sauce coats a spoon.
Salt and pepper to taste. Serve over white rice.
notes: Potatoes go in late on purpose — added at the start they disintegrate.
Soy sauce isn't traditional here; it's doing depth-of-flavor work, and you'll miss it if you skip it.
Curry powder is the one item that may not already be in your pantry. Walmart carries it in the spice aisle.

title: Slow Cooker Honey Garlic Chicken + Rice
blurb: Set it in the morning, eat it when you get home. The hands-off counterpart to #33.

items: 1 tsp cornstarch + 1 tbsp cold water (mixed together)

steps: Soy sauce, honey, and garlic in the slow cooker.
Remove chicken. Stir the cornstarch mixture into the sauce — it thickens in ~2 min.
Chicken and sauce over white rice.
notes: Rice: 1 cup rice + 2 cups water. Bring to a boil, cover, simmer 18 min. Start it when you get home, 20 min before eating.
On HIGH: 3–3½ hrs.
Buy minced garlic in a jar — no chopping.
Want it in 20 minutes with a sticky glaze instead? That's #33.

title: Simple Beef & Tomato Pasta
blurb: Weeknight meat sauce, scaled to one. Half a can of crushed tomatoes is exactly right for a single serving.
steps: Salted water, cook to package directions. Reserve a splash of pasta water before draining.
Olive oil in a skillet over medium-high. Ground beef and onion together, breaking up the beef, ~5–6 min until no pink remains.
Tip off the excess fat. 80/20 renders a lot.
Add crushed tomatoes, garlic powder, Italian seasoning, salt, and pepper. Simmer 8–10 min until slightly thickened.
Add the drained pasta to the sauce and toss. Splash of pasta water if it's tight.
notes: Freeze the remaining half-can of crushed tomatoes, or just double the recipe and have lunch sorted.
Shallots instead of yellow onion works as a 1:1 volume swap. Milder and sweeter, and they cook faster — cut the sauté time or they'll burn.

title: Slow Cooker Pasta e Fagioli
blurb: Italian bean and pasta soup. The pasta goes in at the end — add it early and you'll get mush.

items: 1 cup dry elbow pasta (add at the end — see step 3)

steps: Everything except the pasta into the slow cooker.
Switch to HIGH, cook 30 more min until the pasta is tender.
notes: On HIGH throughout: 3–3½ hrs, then the same 30 min for the pasta.
Standard cans are 15 oz.
Leftovers thicken considerably overnight — loosen with a splash of broth when reheating.

title: Slow Cooker Chicken Tacos
blurb: Three ingredients. The single easiest recipe in this book.

items: Shredded Mexican cheese blend, to serve

steps: Place chicken in the slow cooker.
Pour salsa over the chicken. Sprinkle taco seasoning on top.
Two forks, directly in the pot.
In flour tortillas, topped with shredded cheese.
notes: On HIGH: 3–4 hrs.
Shredding in the pot lets the meat reabsorb the sauce — don't drain it first.

title: Simple Chimichurri
blurb: Bright, garlicky herb sauce. No cooking — just chop and mix. Best made 20+ minutes ahead so the flavors meld.

items: 1 cup fresh parsley, packed, roughly chopped

steps: Finely chop the parsley and garlic. Add both to a bowl.
Stir in vinegar, olive oil, red pepper flakes, oregano, salt, and black pepper. Mix well.
Let sit at room temp at least 20 minutes before serving. This is where the flavor develops.
notes: Cut the vinegar to 1½ tbsp for a milder version.
Keeps in the fridge 4–5 days — flavor improves on day 2.
Food processor works, but pulse in short bursts. It bruises the parsley, darkens it, and it's easy to overshoot into purée. Chimichurri is meant to be rustic — stop before it looks smooth.

title: Air Fryer Baked Potato
blurb: Crisp skin, fluffy interior. Mostly hands-off.

items: Butter, sour cream, shredded cheese, to serve

steps: Scrub and dry completely. Any surface water steams the skin instead of crisping it.
Pierce each potato several times with a fork to let steam escape.
Rub all over with olive oil, then salt and pepper.
A fork should slide into the center with no resistance.
Split open, fluff with a fork, top as you like.
notes: Russets are the right potato. Yukon Gold and red potatoes come out denser and waxier, not fluffy.
Walmart sells russets in 5 lb bags in produce, which is the cheap way to buy them.

title: Air Fryer Frozen Broccoli
blurb: Roasted, not steamed. Cook it straight from frozen.
steps: Straight from the freezer, toss with oil, garlic powder, salt, and pepper.
400°F for 12–13 min total, shaking the basket at the halfway mark.
Parmesan over the top in the last 2 min if using.
notes: Three mistakes, in order of how badly they ruin it: don't thaw first (waterlogged, will never brown), don't crowd the basket (steams instead of roasts), and don't drop the temperature (400°F is what drives off the ice and browns the edges).

title: Air Fryer Frozen Shrimp
blurb: Juicy shrimp in under 10 minutes of cook time. Built for a rice bowl.

items: 1 tbsp olive oil or melted butter

steps: Colander under cold running water 5–7 min until fully thawed. Pat completely dry — this is the difference between texture and steam.
Toss the dry shrimp with oil, garlic powder, paprika, salt, and pepper. Every shrimp evenly coated.
Single layer, no stacking. 400°F for 8 min, flipping at 4 min. Done when pink, opaque, and curled into a loose C.
Lemon juice over the top if using. Serve immediately over rice and veggies.
notes: Doneness by shape: loose C is perfect, tight O is overcooked, straight is undercooked.
Large (21–25 count) or jumbo (16–20 count) work best.
Rice bowl timing: rice first (15–20 min), then veggies in the air fryer, shrimp last — it turns rubbery sitting around.
Fast sauces: mayo + sriracha, or soy sauce + a little honey. Both under a minute.
Seasoning swap: 1 tsp Old Bay, Italian seasoning, or Cajun in place of the paprika and garlic powder.

title: Blueberry Banana Overnight Oats
blurb: No-cook breakfast, assembled the night before. Roughly 15 g protein.
steps: Stir milk, protein powder, and peanut butter together first, until smooth. Doing this before the oats go in is what stops it going lumpy.
Stir in rolled oats until fully coated.
Sliced banana and blueberries. Sweetener if using.
Cover, refrigerate at least 6 hours or overnight.
Straight from the jar. Splash of milk if it's too thick.
notes: Batch-prep 2–3 jars at once — they hold fine for 3 days and make grab-and-go breakfasts trivial.
Frozen blueberries work and are cheaper; they'll bleed a little colour into the oats overnight, which is cosmetic only.

title: Slow Cooker Beef Stew
blurb: Load it and leave it. The one recipe that strains a 2-quart cooker.
steps: All ingredients into the slow cooker.
notes: Chuck roast is the cut — it's what makes stew meat worth the 8 hours.
On HIGH: 4–5 hrs.
Too thin? Stir in 1 tsp cornstarch + 1 tbsp water in the last 30 min.
2-quart slow cooker: this one is a tight fit. Halve the vegetables or use a 4–6 qt cooker.
Prep ahead: cube the potatoes the night before and store them submerged in water in the fridge, then dump them in come morning.

title: Slow Cooker Beef Chili
blurb: Brown the beef the night before and this becomes a genuinely two-minute morning.
steps: Skillet over medium heat, 4–5 min. Drain the fat.
notes: Brown the beef the night before, refrigerate, and add it in the morning — this is the only step standing between you and a two-minute morning.
On HIGH: 3–4 hrs.
Tomato sauce sometimes comes in 8 oz cans — get the 15 oz.

title: Ninja Creami Classic Vanilla
blurb: Rich, creamy vanilla base. The right first Creami recipe — no cooking.
steps: Condensed milk and heavy cream into the Creami pint. Whisk to combine. Add milk and vanilla. Whisk until smooth.
Lid on. Freeze on a level surface 24 hrs minimum. Must be completely solid.
Sit at room temp 5 min. If the top is domed, run the outside under warm water briefly.
ICE CREAM setting. If crumbly, hit RE-SPIN.
Scoop. Store leftovers in the freezer with the lid on.
notes: Condensed milk is doing double duty — sweetener and freeze-point control. It's why this doesn't come out a solid brick. Drop to 125 g if you don't love sweet, up to 175 g if you do.
Stay 1 cm below the max fill line. Overfill and the machine struggles.
Variations: 2 tbsp cocoa powder before freezing for chocolate. Almond extract instead of vanilla. Mix-ins go in on the MIX-IN setting after the first spin.

title: Ninja Creami Yakult
blurb: Tangy, creamy, refreshing — nostalgic Yakult in scoopable form.

items: 195 g Yakult (3 bottles — each is 65 mL/65 g)

steps: Everything into the pint. Whisk until smooth — creamy, not frothy. Let it settle a minute if needed.
Lid on. Freeze 24 hrs on a level surface.
Sit at room temp 5 min. Flatten a domed top with warm water if needed.
LITE ICE CREAM setting. RE-SPIN if crumbly.
Scoop immediately for soft-serve, or refreeze 20–30 min for firmer.
notes: Three bottles fits a 16 oz pint exactly.
The lemon juice sharpens the Yakult tang — it reads as flat without it.

title: Ninja Creami Cheetos Milkshake
blurb: A home version of Baskin Robbins Korea's 치토스 밀크쉐이크 — milkshake and cheese ice cream at once, with chocolate and Cheetos through it.
steps: Whisk softened cream cheese with a splash of the milk until completely lump-free before adding anything else. Lumps here never resolve.
Whisk in remaining milk, heavy cream, condensed milk, and vanilla until smooth.
Lid on, level surface, 24 hrs. Completely solid.
LITE ICE CREAM setting. If crumbly, add a splash of milk and RE-SPIN.
Dig a well in the center. Add chocolate chips and Cheetos Puffs. Run the MIX-IN setting.
notes: Cheetos Puffs, not Crunchy — the puffs are much closer to the Cheetos balls in the original.
Serve immediately. The Cheetos soften fast once they're in; this is the one Creami recipe that doesn't keep. Add them at the mix-in stage, never to the base.
The cream cheese is what captures both halves of the original flavor — the milkshake and the cheese ice cream — in a single base.

title: Kimchi Fried Rice (Kimchi Bokkeumbap)
blurb: Ground pork, sour kimchi, and cold rice in one pan, finished with a runny fried egg. The best thing to do with kimchi that's gone too sour to eat straight.
appleNote: Kimchi paste and gochujang both routinely contain apple or Korean pear. This recipe stacks both in a single pan.

items: 150 g napa cabbage kimchi, well-fermented, roughly chopped
2 tbsp kimchi juice, from the jar

steps: Take the cold rice out of the fridge and break the clumps apart with your fingers or a fork until the grains are loose. Cold rice fries; warm rice turns to paste.
Neutral oil in a large skillet over medium-high. Add the pork and break it up. Cook 5 min until no pink remains and the edges are browned. Don't drain the fat — it carries the flavor.
Add the chopped kimchi. Cook 3–4 min, stirring, until it darkens and smells sweet rather than raw. This is the step most people rush, and it's where the flavor comes from.
Push everything to one side. Gochujang, soy sauce, and sugar into the bare pan. Stir 30 seconds until fragrant, then mix through the pork and kimchi.
Toss until every grain is coated orange-red. Pour in the kimchi juice and keep tossing 2–3 min. Press the rice flat for the last minute to get a few crispy bits.
Push the rice aside or use a second small pan. Fry the egg over medium heat 2–3 min, white set and yolk still runny.
Off the heat, drizzle the sesame oil over the rice and toss once. Plate it, egg on top, green onion scattered over. Break the yolk into the rice as you eat.
notes: Sour kimchi is correct kimchi here. Fizzy, soft, past-its-prime kimchi has the depth this dish is built on. Fresh kimchi tastes flat and stays crunchy. If yours is still mild, leave the open jar at room temperature 1–2 days first.
No day-old rice? Spread fresh rice in a thin layer on a plate and refrigerate uncovered 30 min. Do not skip this — fresh rice gives you a wet clump.
Sesame oil goes in off the heat. It scorches over direct flame and turns bitter.
Shopping: gochujang is at Walmart in the international aisle. Kimchi is in refrigerated produce near the tofu, though H Mart has better selection and faster turnover.
Swaps: Spam (150 g, diced, browned first) or bacon in place of the pork. Skip the protein entirely and it still works — add an extra ½ tsp sesame oil.

title: Overnight Sourdough Bread (Pizza Stone)
blurb: Mix and fold today, bake tomorrow. Steam under a hot pizza stone gives you a crackly crust without a Dutch oven. 70% hydration, 20% starter.

items: 100 g active sourdough starter, fed and bubbly

steps: The morning before you plan to mix, feed your starter and let it sit at room temperature until doubled, domed, and full of bubbles — usually 4–6 hours. It's ready when a spoonful dropped in water floats.

Combine the water and starter in a large bowl, stirring until the starter loosens into the water. Add the flour and mix by hand until no dry flour remains — shaggy and rough, not smooth. Cover and rest 30 min.
Sprinkle the salt over the dough with a small splash of water. Squeeze and fold in the bowl about 2 minutes until the salt disappears and the dough feels smoother.

Over the next 2 hours, do 4 sets of folds, 30 minutes apart: wet one hand, grab a side of the dough, stretch it up and fold it over the top; turn the bowl a quarter turn and repeat 3 more times per set. Cover between sets.
After the last fold, cover and leave at room temperature until the dough looks puffy and jiggly and has grown by about half — roughly 2–3 more hours, longer in a cool kitchen.
Turn the dough onto a lightly floured counter. Pull the edges underneath itself repeatedly, rotating as you go, until you have a tight ball with a taut surface.
Place seam-side up in a flour-dusted bowl lined with a clean kitchen towel, or a floured banneton. Cover and refrigerate 12–15 hours.

Next day, set the pizza stone on a middle rack with a metal pan or cast iron skillet on a lower rack. Preheat to 475°F for at least 45 minutes — the stone needs time to heat through. Put a kettle on near the end of that window.

Take the dough straight from the fridge; cold dough scores cleaner. Turn it onto parchment, dust the top with flour, and slash about ½ inch deep with a sharp knife or razor. Slide parchment and dough onto the hot stone.
Working quickly with an oven mitt, pour 1 cup of just-boiled water into the pan below — it billows steam fast, so stand back. Shut the door immediately and bake 20 minutes.
Remove the steam pan. Bake 20–25 minutes more, until the crust is deep golden-brown and the loaf sounds hollow when you tap the bottom.
Move to a wire rack and cool at least 1 hour before slicing. It's still cooking from residual heat — cutting early makes the crumb gummy.
notes: Bread flour gives the best structure and chew; all-purpose works as a 1:1 swap with a slightly softer crumb.
No scale? 10 g salt is roughly 1½–2 tsp fine sea salt. Weighing is worth it for bread — volume varies a lot by grain size.
The steam step is intense. Oven mitt on, stand back when you pour.
Kitchen temperature moves fermentation more than the clock does. Go by how puffy and jiggly the dough looks, not the exact minute.
Keeps cut-side-down at room temp 2–3 days, or slice and freeze what you won't eat soon.
First loaf doesn't need to look perfect — a lopsided crack or uneven crumb won't affect the taste.

title: Sticky Honey Garlic Chicken Bites
blurb: Bite-sized thighs seared hard, then tossed in a honey-soy glaze that reduces onto the chicken in about 90 seconds. One pan. The fast counterpart to #17.

items: 360 g (0.8 lb) boneless skinless chicken thighs, cut into 1-inch chunks
2 tsp minced garlic, from the jar

steps: Cut the thighs into 1-inch chunks and pat dry with paper towels. Wet chicken steams instead of browning. Toss with cornstarch, salt, and pepper until every piece has a thin dusty coating.
Stir together honey, soy sauce, garlic, water, and rice vinegar in a small bowl. Set it next to the stove — once the chicken is cooked this moves fast.
Heat the oil in a large skillet over medium-high until it shimmers. Add the chicken in a single layer, not crowded. Leave it alone for 4 minutes — moving it early tears the crust off.
Flip the pieces and cook 3–4 more minutes until browned all over and cooked through (165°F, or cut one open — no pink).

Turn the heat down to medium-low. This matters: honey scorches on high heat and turns bitter. Pour the sauce in and toss constantly for 60–90 seconds until it goes from watery to glossy and clings to the chicken.
Off the heat. Scatter green onion and sesame seeds over the top. Serve over white rice and spoon any glaze left in the pan over it.
notes: Cornstarch goes on the chicken, not in the sauce — it does both jobs at once. It gives you a browned crust in the pan, and the starch that comes loose is what thickens the glaze. No separate slurry.
The rice vinegar isn't optional in spirit. 3 tbsp honey with nothing sharp against it tastes flat and cloying. A squeeze of lemon works if you don't have it.
0.8 lb is a small batch for a big skillet, which is good — crowding is the main failure mode. Past 1.5 lbs, sear in two batches.
Heat variation: ½ tsp gochujang or a squirt of sriracha into the sauce.
Want it hands-off instead? That's #17.

title: Simple Budae Jjigae (Army Stew)
blurb: One-pot Korean army stew — Spam, hot dog, kimchi, baked beans, and ramen noodles in a medium-spicy broth, finished with melted cheese.
allergens: pork, wheat, soy, dairy, egg (check the ramen)
appleNote: Both the kimchi and the gochujang commonly use apple or Korean pear as a sweetener, and this dish stacks both.

items: 100 g Spam, sliced into bite-size pieces
1 hot dog, sliced on a diagonal
2 tbsp kimchi juice, from the jar
½ instant ramen noodle brick (set the seasoning packet aside)

steps: In a small bowl, stir the gochujang, gochugaru, soy sauce, garlic, and sugar together with a splash of the water or broth until smooth.

In a shallow pot or skillet, arrange the Spam, hot dog, kimchi, baked beans, and onion in sections rather than mixing them together. This is the classic budae jjigae look, and it makes it easier to fish out what you want first.
Spoon the sauce mixture over the top. Pour the water or broth and the kimchi juice in around the edges.
Bring to a boil over medium-high heat, then reduce to a simmer for 8–10 minutes so the flavors meld and the kimchi softens.
Nestle in the ramen brick. Simmer 3–4 minutes, separating the noodles with chopsticks or tongs as they soften, until just tender.
Lay the cheese slice on top of the noodles. Turn off the heat and let it melt for a minute before serving.
Scatter the green onion over the top. Serve straight from the pot, bubbling.
notes: Shopping: Walmart has Spam, hot dogs, baked beans, ramen, and American cheese. Gochujang and gochugaru are in Walmart's international aisle in a pinch, but H Mart has better selection. Kimchi: Walmart's refrigerated international section or H Mart.
No baked beans on hand? Skip them. They're a common Americanized addition, not traditional.
Rice cakes (tteok) or sliced Korean fish cake are classic add-ins if you want to expand it later.
Freeze the unused ramen half for next time.
Scales up cleanly to a shared pot — multiply everything and use a wider pan so it isn't crowded.
